paras: The lynching of Eli Davie was the killing of a Black man, charged with burning a tobacco barn near Fulton, Kentucky, who was taken from a train by masked men at Woodland Mills, Obion County, Tennessee, early on March 15, 1888, and hanged. He was in the custody of a constable who was carrying him to the county jail at Hickman, Kentucky, after an examining trial at Fulton, where open threats to lynch him had been made. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, and a Union City dispatch carried the story from Indiana to California.

According to the Union City dispatch, the barn of Lewis Browder, a farmer about six miles from Fulton, burned on March 6, a loss put at $3,000. The Hickman Courier dated the fire to March 5 and valued the tobacco lost at about $600. Two other houses nearby had recently burned, one with a son of William Campbell inside, and though the Courier did not know the prisoner was accused of those fires, it wrote that the community was "wrought up to a high feeling against the offender."
After a reward was offered, Davie was found hiding in a straw stack and arrested by "four other negroes," the Memphis Appeal reported.

At an examining trial before Esquire Bonz at Fulton on Wednesday, Davie pleaded not guilty, was held for the circuit court and, unable to give $500 bond, was committed to the county jail. Open threats of lynching followed in Fulton, and County Attorney Murrell appealed for the law to take its course.

Constable W. J. Winstead announced that the prisoner would stay overnight in the city lock-up while planning to take him to Hickman on the night train. The lynchers learned of the plan, and when the train stopped at Woodland Mills about 2:30 a.m. Thursday, masked men boarded it. In the account taken from Winstead, six men boarded, and he drew his pistol but was seized from behind. The Courier described about a dozen men with shotguns and pistols in the car and as many outside, and said Winstead was still pleading with them when the train pulled away.
The men took Davie to an oak tree about 300 yards from the depot and hanged him, and he was found there later that morning.

An inquest held the same morning returned a verdict that "an unknown negro" had been found and had come to his death at the hands of unknown parties. The Union City correspondent added that although the hanging took place in Obion County, "the Kentucky boys did the job." No report of arrests, an indictment or a prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Hickman Courier carried the fullest account on its local page the next day under the headline "ANOTHER MOB." It praised Winstead's efforts and explained local anger over the fires but passed no judgment on the lynchers.

Elsewhere a Union City special to the Nashville American ran in the Indianapolis Journal and St. Paul Daily Globe on March 16 and the Beatrice Daily Express on March 17, as "Negro Incendiary Lynched," "Lynched for Arson" and "An Incendiary Lynched." A shorter version, saying only that Davie was found "ornamenting the limb of a tree," ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and Nevada's Silver State. The Memphis Appeal printed the longest form of the dispatch on March 17 as "LYNCHING NEAR HICKMAN, KY. A Negro Barn Burner Hanged Up by a Mob."

These papers treated the charge as settled, and the St. Paul Globe dropped the claim of an accident, saying only "He confessed his guilt." Later brief notices in the Semi-weekly South Kentuckian and the Kanabec County Times named him "Eli Nary" and "Eli Daire."

The officer-based dispatch counted six masked men; the local Courier counted about a dozen, with as many outside. The Courier also put the seizure on the 4 o'clock train between Woodland Mills and State Line rather than at the depot, and the South Kentuckian placed it near Fulton.

Reports of a confession were secondhand: the wire said he called the fire accidental, while the Courier wrote only that he was said to have confessed. His name was printed as Davie, Davey, Davis, Nary and Daire.

reader.title: Lynching of Eli Davie
bases: Masked men took a Black prisoner from a constable on a train and hanged him from a tree (A1, A6).

Six or more masked men took Davie from an officer and hanged him (A6, A1), acting on a barn-burning charge after open lynching threats at Fulton (A1); the inquest found death at the hands of unknown parties (A6).
The local Hickman Courier (A1) and the independent Union City dispatch (A6, A2) agree on the seizure from the train and the killing.

accounts.label: Officer's account via Union City dispatch
accounts.gist: Six masked men boarded the train at Woodland Mills about 2:30 a.m.; Winstead drew his pistol but was seized from behind, and the prisoner was hanged from a tree about 300 yards from the depot.

accounts.label: Hickman Courier (local)
accounts.gist: After open lynching threats at Fulton, about a dozen armed, masked men, with as many outside, halted the 4 o'clock train between Woodland Mills and State Line and took the prisoner despite Winstead's pleas.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: An unknown negro came to his death at the hands of unknown parties.

framing.detail: The Hickman Courier headed its local report 'ANOTHER MOB', praised the constable's efforts and recounted the county attorney's plea for the law without editorial judgment of the lynchers.
Distant papers ran the Union City special as 'Negro Incendiary Lynched', 'Lynched for Arson', 'A Barn-Burner Lynched' and 'An Incendiary Lynched', calling him a 'negro barn burner'.
The Memphis Appeal's 'A Negro Barn Burner Hanged Up by a Mob' described the body 'ornamenting the limb of an oak tree' while reporting the confession as accidental and the inquest verdict.

Charged with burning one tobacco barn, Lewis Browder's, near Fulton, Ky.; said to have confessed but called it accidental
Masked, armed men, six (wire) or about a dozen with as many outside (Courier); the dispatch said 'the Kentucky boys did the job'
An ad hoc mob formed after open lynching threats at Fulton; no organized band is named
Lynching on March 15; March 6 (or 5) is the date of the barn fire
